{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:

Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.

This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[Hokkaido|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|ja|姥神大神宮}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[August 9]], [[August 10|10]], and [[August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Festival]] via the [[Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[2019]] ({{ill|Heisei|ja|平成}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū#History|ja|姥神大神宮}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[1644]] ({{ill|Shōhō|ja|正保}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[1816]] ({{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[1862]] ({{ill|Bunkyū|ja|文久}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[Empress Jingū]], crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|ja|宝暦}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].
