==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of [[:en:Ubagami Daijingū|Ubagami Daijingu]], which is considered the oldest shrine in [[:en:Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|Esashi, Hokkaido]], [[:en:Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Hiyama District, Hokkaido]], [[:en:Hokkaido|Hokkaido]].
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: [[:en:August 9|August 9]], [[:en:August 10|August 10]], and [[:en:August 11|August 11]]. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by [[:en:Matsuri float|dashi]] (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the [[:en:Kitamaebune|Kitamaebune]] maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the [[:en:Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. On March 19, 2019 ([[:en:Heisei era|Heisei]] 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to [[:en:Shōhō|1644]] (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ([[:en:Culture|Bunka]] 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ([[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyū]] 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ([[:en:Genji era|Genji]] 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.
=== Types of Yama === During the festival, the following 13 Yama parade through the town: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Yama Name !! Figure !! Neighborhood !! The oldest Yama figure is the [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] figure from Jingū Yama, which was created in 1754 ([[:en:Hōreki|Hōreki]] 4) and is designated as a Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q24896695]] Wikidata name: Ubagami Daijingū Togyosai [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ([[:en:Ubagami Daijingū|Ubagami Daijingū]]), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from [[:en:August 9|August 9]], [[:en:August 10|10]], and [[:en:August 11|11]], is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the [[:en:Kitamaebune|Kitamaebune]] trade routes. On March 19, [[:en:2019|2019]] ([[:en:Heisei era|Heisei]] 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in [[:en:Ubagami Daijingū|Ubagami Daijingū#History]].
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year [[:en:1644|1644]] ([[:en:Shōhō|Shōhō]] 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By [[:en:1816|1816]] ([[:en:Culture|Bunka]] 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until [[:en:1862|1862]] ([[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyū]] 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From [[:en:1962|1962]] (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || [[:en:Date Masamune|Date Masamune]] || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || [[:en:Katō Kiyomasa|Katō Kiyomasa]] || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || [[:en:Benkei|Musashibō Benkei]] || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || [[:en:Yamato Takeru|Yamato Takeru]] || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || [[:en:Tokugawa Mitsukuni|Tokugawa Mitsukuni]] || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || [[:en:Emperor Jimmu|Emperor Jimmu]] || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || [[:en:Ebisu (mythology)|Ebisu]] || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || [[:en:Takeda Shingen|Takeda Shingen]] || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]], crafted in [[:en:Hōreki|Hōreki]] 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of [[:en:Ubagami Daijingū|Ubagami Daijingu]], which is considered the oldest shrine in [[:en:Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|Esashi, Hokkaido]], [[:en:Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Hiyama District, Hokkaido]], [[:en:Hokkaido|Hokkaido]].
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: [[:en:August 9|August 9]], [[:en:August 10|August 10]], and [[:en:August 11|August 11]]. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by [[:en:Matsuri float|dashi]] (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the [[:en:Kitamaebune|Kitamaebune]] maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the [[:en:Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. On March 19, 2019 ([[:en:Heisei era|Heisei]] 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to [[:en:Shōhō|1644]] (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ([[:en:Culture|Bunka]] 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ([[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyū]] 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ([[:en:Genji era|Genji]] 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.
=== Types of Yama === During the festival, the following 13 Yama parade through the town: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Yama Name !! Figure !! Neighborhood !! revision.text:
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q24896695]] Wikidata name: Ubagami Daijingū Togyosai [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

revision.text:
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q24896695]] Wikidata name: Ubagami Daijingū Togyosai [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

The oldest Yama figure is the {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} figure from Jingū Yama, which was created in 1754 ({{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4) and is designated as a Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property.

revision.text:
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q24896695]] Wikidata name: Ubagami Daijingū Togyosai [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.

The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]]
{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

The oldest Yama figure is the {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} figure from Jingū Yama, which was created in 1754 ({{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4) and is designated as a Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property.

{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].

==Merged second translation== {{Multiple issues | Refimprove = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Too many images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the annual grand festival of {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingu}}, which is considered the oldest shrine in {{ill|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|en|Esashi, Hokkaido (Hiyama)|WD=Q1348738|lt=Esashi, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|en|Hiyama District, Hokkaido|WD=Q1186011|lt=Hiyama District, Hokkaido}}, {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaido}}.
== Overview == The festival, which has a history of over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="注">As of 2024</ref>, takes place annually over three days: {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=August 11}}. It is regarded as the oldest festival in Hokkaido. The festival consists of a procession of {{ill|mikoshi|ja|御輿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/mikoshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神輿}} (portable shrines) followed by {{ill|Matsuri float|en|Matsuri float|WD=Q11470974|lt=dashi}} (festival floats), known locally as "Yama," parading through the town. Influenced by the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune}} maritime trade, the festival is said to inherit cultural elements from the {{ill|Gion Matsuri|en|Gion Matsuri|WD=Q979873|lt=Gion Festival}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. On March 19, 2019 ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei}} 31), it was designated as an {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 民俗文化財|1=Folk Cultural Property of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q24895900}} of Hokkaido.
For the origin of the festival, see {{ill|Ubagami Daijingu#History|ja|姥神大神宮#歴史|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ubagami Daijingu#History|1=Ubagami Daijin-gū shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3547609}}.
== History == The origin of the festival is uncertain, but it is commonly believed to date back to {{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=1644}} (Shōhō 1), the year when Ubagami Daijingu was relocated to its current site{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}.
According to the 1816 ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka}} 13) {{ill|Fujieda Family Documents|ja|藤枝家文書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujieda Family Documents|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} "Shachi Denki Hikae"{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=10}}, the festival initially alternated annually with the {{ill|Benzaiten shrines|lt=Benten Shrine|ja|弁天社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Benzaiten shrines|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 弁才天}} on {{ill|Kamome Island|ja|鴎島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamome Island|1=Kamome Island|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q23997926}}, the current location of Itsukushima Shrine. Festivals were held from August 14 to 16 each year. A later Fujieda document, "Gengi 1 Nen Shichigatsu Ubagamigu Yomiya Reisai Nikki," describes that the alternating festivals continued until 1862 ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū}} 2){{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=11}}. This document also mentions that in the same year, the two festivals were separated, and the festival of Ubagami Daijingu began exclusively the following year ({{ill|Genji era|en|Genji era|WD=Q1325419|lt=Genji}} 1).
Following the separation, the Ubagami Daijingu Togyo Festival continued, although the festival period changed several times. Until 1962 (Showa 37), the festival was held from August 20 to 23. However, based on a town-wide survey, the schedule was changed to the current dates from the following year{{Sfn|祭図録|1999|page=12}}.
== Dashi (Yama) == In Esashi Town, festival floats are called "Yama" and are carefully preserved by local neighborhoods. The Yama, following the mikoshi procession, are considered an essential part of the festival. The tradition of including Yama in the Ubagami Daijingu festival is said to date back to the mid-19th century{{Sfn|江差姥神大神宮祭礼写真集|2002|pages=110-111}}.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Ubagami Daijin-gū Togyosai]][[ja:姥神大神宮渡御祭]]
{{Multiple issues | Sources needed = July 2019 | Original research = September 2019 | Not encyclopedic = September 2019 | Overly detailed = September 2019 | Excessive images = March 2019 }} '''Ubagami Daijingū Togyo Festival''' (姥神大神宮渡御祭) is the grand festival (例大祭) of [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaido's]] oldest shrine, [[Ubagami Daijingū]] ({{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū|1=Ubagami Daijingū}}), located in [[Esashi, Hiyama District, Hokkaido|Esashi Town, Hiyama District]].
== Overview == The festival, held over three days annually from {{ill|August 9|en|August 9|WD=Q2782|lt=August 9|1=August 9}}, {{ill|August 10|en|August 10|WD=Q2779|lt=10|1=August 10}}, and {{ill|August 11|en|August 11|WD=Q2778|lt=11|1=August 11}}, is considered the oldest in Hokkaido with a history spanning over 380 years<ref name="ubagami-history" group="note">As of 2024</ref>. The event includes a [[Mikoshi]] procession followed by parade floats (referred to as "Yama" in the town), which travel through the town. This tradition is influenced by the cultural heritage of the {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} [[Gion Matsuri|Gion Festival]] via the {{ill|Kitamaebune|en|Kitamaebune|WD=Q3440099|lt=Kitamaebune|1=Kitamaebune}} trade routes. On March 19, {{ill|2019|en|2019|WD=Q25274|lt=2019|1=2019}} ({{ill|Heisei era|en|Heisei era|WD=Q234510|lt=Heisei|1=Heisei era}} 31), the festival was designated as an [[Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido|Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido]].
The origins of the festival can be referenced in {{ill|Ubagami Daijingū|en|Ubagami Daijingū|WD=Q3547609|lt=Ubagami Daijingū#History|1=Ubagami Daijingū}}.
== History == The festival’s origins are unclear, but common belief ties it to the year {{ill|1644|en|1644|WD=Q6920|lt=1644|1=1644}} ({{ill|Shōhō|en|Shōhō|WD=Q1146192|lt=Shōhō|1=Shōhō}} 1), when Ubagami Daijingū was relocated to its current site<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref>.
By {{ill|1816|en|1816|WD=Q6953|lt=1816|1=1816}} ({{ill|Culture|en|Culture|WD=Q11042|lt=Bunka|1=Culture}} 13), records from the Fujieda family in the document “Shrine Grounds Chronicle”<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=10}}</ref> state that the festival alternated yearly between Ubagami Daijingū and Benten Shrine on [[Kamome Island, Esashi|Kamome Island]] (present-day {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja|厳島神社 (江差町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine (Kamome Island)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) during August 14–16. This practice continued until {{ill|1862|en|1862|WD=Q7698|lt=1862|1=1862}} ({{ill|Bunkyū|en|Bunkyū|WD=Q730266|lt=Bunkyū|1=Bunkyū}} 2), when the two shrines’ festivals were separated<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=11}}</ref>.
From {{ill|1962|en|1962|WD=Q2764|lt=1962|1=1962}} (Showa 37), the festival dates were August 20–23 but were changed to the current schedule through a town-wide survey<ref>{{Sfn|Festival Record|1999|page=12}}</ref>.
== Floats ("Yama") == In Esashi, the parade floats are referred to as "Yama" and are cherished by each neighborhood. The floats follow the mikoshi procession. This practice began in the mid-19th century and continues to this day<ref>{{Sfn|Ubagami Daijingū Festival Photo Collection|2002|pages=110-111}}</ref>.
=== Types of Floats === The festival features 13 floats, each unique in design and origin:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! Float Name !! Character !! Neighborhood !! Notes |- | Masamune Yama || {{ill|Date Masamune|en|Date Masamune|WD=Q311183|lt=Date Masamune|1=Date Masamune}} || Shinchi, Maruyama, Midorigaoka || |- | Kiyomasa Yama || {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|WD=Q1069843|lt=Katō Kiyomasa|1=Katō Kiyomasa}} || Honmachi || |- | Genji Yama || {{ill|Benkei|en|Benkei|WD=Q316898|lt=Musashibō Benkei|1=Benkei}} || Uenomachi || |- | Shōmu Yama || {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} || Hashimoto || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Yo Yama || [[:en:Ōishi Kuranosuke|Ōishi Kuranosuke]] || Mojiri || |- | Gikō Yama || {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni|1=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} || Minami-hama, Kashiwa, Minami-gaoka || |- | Matsuhōmaru || No character, features children as rowers || Kaigan, Jinya || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Kusunoki Yama || [[Kusunoki Masashige]] || Tsunohana || |- | Hōnen Yama || {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} || Ubakami || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Ebisu Yama || {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|en|Ebisu (mythology)|WD=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu|1=Ebisu (mythology)}} || Nakauta || Esashi Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Toyosaka Yama || [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] || Toyokawa || |- | Jingū Yama || {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} || Atago || Hokkaido Tangible Folk Cultural Property |- | Shinei Yama || {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|WD=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen|1=Takeda Shingen}} || Shinei || |}
The oldest float is Jingū Yama’s figure of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|WD=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}}, crafted in {{ill|Hōreki|en|Hōreki|WD=Q1194397|lt=Hōreki|1=Hōreki}} 4 (1754). It is a designated Tangible Folk Cultural Property of Hokkaido.
Floats like Shōmu Yama feature unique karakuri mechanisms that allow movement. Matsuhōmaru, the only "ship float," is built in the style of a traditional Japanese ship.
For more information, visit the [https://esashi.town/tourism Ubakami Festival Website].
